question.text: Convertible Arbitrage, as practised by Category III AIFs, is best described as:

answer.text: Closing all positions in convertible securities to avoid market risk
Taking a long position in convertible securities of a company and simultaneously taking a short position in the equity shares of the same company
Buying only the equity shares of the company and holding them to maturity
Selling listed equity options on an index and holding cash

explanation.text: The Logic: Convertible arbitrage seeks to exploit the relative pricing between a company's convertible securities (such as convertible bonds or convertible preference shares) and its underlying equity. The classic structure involves going long the convertible security and simultaneously going short the equity shares of the same issuer, so that the position seeks to profit from the convertible's pricing characteristics while reducing exposure to broad equity-price movements in the issuer's stock. The Trap: Closing all positions is the opposite of running a strategy. Holding only the long equity position offers no arbitrage element and full directional exposure. Selling index options is an unrelated options strategy and does not capture the long-convertible / short-equity construction that defines convertible arbitrage. Note: The cited workbook chapter on Category III investment strategies describes convertible arbitrage as a long position in convertible securities combined with a simultaneous short position in the same company's equity shares. The earlier "delta-hedging" / delta-proportional formulation that this question previously tested is not used in the cited chapter; the framing above is aligned with the workbook's simpler description.
